name: Rules Students Can Follow
title: Rules Students Can Follow
answer: A clear acceptable use policy for AI gives students and parents rules they can actually follow, instead of a ban or informal guidelines that are hard to sustain. Its most useful part is often a simple scale of allowed AI use marked on each assignment, so students know what is permitted. This matters because it shifts the question from whether AI was used to whether it was used at the allowed level, which is fairer and does not rely on detection scores as proof.

crumbs.name: Privacy, Safety, and the Human Review Rule

sections.body: Districts need an acceptable use policy that covers AI and is written in language students and parents can follow. Many districts began with a ban on student use or with a few informal guidelines, and the text says both were hard to sustain (McGuire et al., 2026). A ban can push use out of sight, while informal guidelines can mean different rules in every classroom. A clear policy, drafted with teachers, students, and parents and reviewed each year, works better than either approach. The policy's most useful part is often a simple scale of allowed AI use for each assignment, marked by the teacher on the assignment itself.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the teacher marks the allowed AI level on the assignment, so there is no guessing about what is permitted. A research paper might be marked for feedback on a draft only, while a brainstorming exercise might allow AI for ideas. Figure 3.7 shows a five level scale that works from upper elementary through high school. The scale changes the conversation about cheating by asking whether the student used AI at the level the assignment allowed. That question is fairer and avoids leaning on AI detection scores, which are not proof.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites McGuire et al., 2026 for the finding that many districts started with a ban on student use or a few informal guidelines and then found both hard to sustain. It also refers to Figure 3.7, which shows a five level scale that works from upper elementary through high school. No other study, figure, or finding is given for this idea. The support here is the cited district experience and the practical scale shown in the figure.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are that a ban pushes use out of sight and informal guidelines create different rules in every classroom. AI detection scores are not proof, so they should not be the basis for judging whether a student followed the rules. The decision about the allowed level for each assignment stays with the teacher, who marks it on the assignment itself. The policy itself should be drafted with teachers, students, and parents and reviewed each year. Students still make the choice to use AI within those rules, just as citing a source is a choice with rules.
